newsitem.title: USA: US markets up, but no runaway rally, on jobs data.
newsitem.headline: US markets up, but no runaway rally, on jobs data.

text.p: U.S. bonds, stocks and the dollar advanced after a report on January U.S. employment soothed fears of very strong job growth and rising inflation.
The report calmed fears the Federal Reserve might tighten monetary policy soon, analysts said, but a dearth of evidence to support an eventual easing blocked an overwhelming rally.
"The markets reacted very positively to the January employment data," said Elliott Platt, managing director and director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp.

"First, the figures suggested that the Fed is on hold at least until the March (Federal Open Market Committee) meeting," Platt said. "Also, as we got closer to the release of this number, economists were ratcheting up their estimates of payroll growth. The most recent surveys had higher consensus estimates than the surveys taken a week ago."
U.S. Treasury prices, which moved higher ahead of the report, scored further gains after it was released.
For a time, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up more than a point, its yield falling as low as 6.69 percent before bouncing back to about 6.7 percent shortly after noon.
The stock market also advanced when it opened an hour after the release of the January employment report.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed just over 95 points to 6868.50, before settling back to 6825.40 up 51.96.

The dollar also rallied after the employment report before a mild bout of profit taking pushed it lower ahead of this weekend's meeting of financial officials from the Group of Seven leading industrial nations. U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said that while the strong dollar is in the U.S. interest, U.S. officials are willing to discuss weaker currencies with nations concerned.
"The dollar did better off the number because no one (concentrated on) the headline (figure)," said David Durrant, senior currency strategist at consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc.
"They looked at the hourly earnings (and those) simply (said) to us that inflation is not a factor," he added.

U.S. payrolls grew by 271,000 jobs in January after 261,000 new jobs were added in December, the Labor Department reported. Meanwhile, the unemployment rate rose to 5.4 percent from 5.3 percent in December, the government said.
The length of the average workweek also shrank. The Labor Department tied that contraction -- especially pronounced in the construction industry -- to harsh winter weather.
Especially pleasing to the markets was the very slight rise in average hourly earnings, participants said.
The Labor Department said average hourly earnings -- a key measure of wage pressures -- rose just one cent, after more substantial increases in November and December.
"The most important thing was that hourly wages were up just one cent," said Joseph Barthel, chief investment strategist at Fahnestock & Co.
Platt said the markets gained on "relief" and short-covering trades.

"The market got what it wanted, especially from the hourly earnings number which was very encouraging on inflation," said Guy Truicko, portfolio manager at Unity Management. "Bonds rallied and stocks followed."
But analysts said the markets would probably continue to trade near the top of their current ranges, not yet ready to move up to new high ground.
"The (Treasury) market will stall here because the payroll data certainly do not harbor indications of weakness in the U.S. economy or any imminent Fed easing," said Platt.

"We've been in a trading range for a couple of weeks and we're up at the top of that range right now," added Truiko. "It seems like when we get up to the top of the range, there's been a wall; so 6900 (on the Dow) could be a key area."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679 ))
